title: Building a restaurant catering menu callers understand
seoTitle: Restaurant catering menu that callers understand | ROAL
description: Build a catering menu with clear packages, plain prices, and wording that works on the phone. Cut confusion before the order is placed.
question: How do I make a restaurant catering menu easy for callers to understand over the phone?
answer: Make your restaurant catering menu phone-friendly by using simple package names, clear serving counts, and easy add-on choices. Put the most common questions up front: how many people it feeds, what comes in the tray, when it’s ready, and whether utensils or setup items are included. Keep the language short so callers can place a catering order without guessing.
summary: You’ll learn how to turn a catering menu into simple phone language that callers can order from quickly.
intro:
A restaurant catering menu works best when it is easy to say out loud. Callers should be able to hear the package, understand how many people it feeds, and know what comes with it without asking three follow-up questions.

If your menu is hard to explain on the phone, the order slows down and staff spend time translating it. A cleaner menu helps your team, helps callers, and gives an AI phone host like ROAL clearer choices to read back and confirm.

sections.h2: What should a catering menu say first?
sections.body:
Start with the details callers ask for most. Put the serving size, the main items, and the price at the top of every catering item. If you sell a tray or package, say exactly what it feeds in plain language like “feeds 8–10” or “serves 12.”

A caller should not have to hunt for basics. For example, a line like “Chicken parm tray — feeds 10, includes bread, $89” is much easier to order than a long paragraph.

Use this order for each item:
1. Name of the tray or package
2. How many people it feeds
3. What it includes
4. Price
5. Add-ons or swaps

If you use ROAL, the phone host can read from your live menu and repeat these details back on the call. That matters because callers often place catering orders while driving, working, or standing in line. Short, clean wording keeps the conversation moving.

sections.h2: How do I write catering items so callers don’t get confused?
sections.body:
Write the menu like you speak. Skip long descriptions and full sentences. Use short labels that sound natural on a call.

Here is a simple format that works well for a restaurant catering menu:

| Menu item | Phone-friendly version |
|---|---|
| Party sandwich tray | Sandwich tray, feeds 10, mixed cold sandwiches, chips included |
| Pasta tray | Baked ziti tray, feeds 8 to 10, garlic bread included |
| Breakfast platter | Breakfast platter, feeds 12, eggs, bacon, home fries |
| Salad tray | Garden salad tray, feeds 8, dressing on the side |

A few rules help a lot:
- Use the same name on the menu, on the phone, and on the ticket.
- Put sizes in the same place every time.
- If a tray has choices, keep the choices simple: chicken or eggplant, mild or hot, small or large.
- Say what is included and what costs extra.

ROAL can take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the live menu, then send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That means the caller hears one version of the menu, not a patched-together version from memory.

sections.h2: What details should be on every catering item card?
sections.body:
Think of each item card as a phone script, not just a printed menu line. The card should answer the questions staff hear every day. For catering, those usually are: how much food, what is included, whether utensils are included, and how early the order should be placed.

Use a short checklist for each item:
- Serving count
- Main components
- Sides or bread included
- Utensils, plates, and napkins included or extra
- Any temperature note, like hot or cold
- Any cutoff time or prep note

Example:
“Chicken parm tray
Feeds 10
Includes bread and salad
Utensils available on request
Needs 2 hours notice”

That is easier for a caller to understand than a paragraph hidden on a PDF. It also gives your staff a cleaner handoff when the order comes in. If a question is tricky, ROAL can hand it to staff with a summary, which is useful for allergy-sensitive requests, manager requests, and complicated catering changes.

If you carry sold-out items, mark them clearly. ROAL does not offer items marked sold out, so the phone host stays aligned with what your kitchen can actually make.

sections.h2: How do I price catering without making the phone messy?
sections.body:
Keep the pricing structure simple. Callers understand menus faster when prices follow a pattern. For example, use one base price for the tray, then clearly list add-ons instead of hiding them in notes.

A simple setup might look like this:
- Tray price: $68
- Extra bread: $6
- Extra sauce: $4
- Utensil pack: included
- Extra utensils: $3

Here is a worked example you can swap for your own numbers. Say a catering order is a pasta tray at $68, extra chicken at $14, and delivery prep items at $6. The caller hears the total as $88 before any tax or local charge your restaurant already uses. If your order is different, plug in your own prices and keep the math visible.

This matters because callers do not want to do mental math while ordering food for 12 people. Clear pricing also helps with phone order speed. If a caller asks for a quote, the phone host can confirm the order back before the ticket goes to the kitchen screen.

For owners comparing phone options, [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) is worth a look. A phone model that charges only when a confirmed order reaches the kitchen can feel very different from a fixed monthly fee.

sections.h2: What should callers hear when they place a catering order?
sections.body:
The phone script should be short, calm, and repeatable. A good catering call usually follows the same path every time: size of order, item choice, pickup time, name, phone number, and any notes.

A simple script line can sound like this:
“Sure, I can help with catering. How many people are you feeding, and what date do you need it for?”

Then keep going with plain follow-up questions:
1. Which tray or package would you like?
2. Do you want any sides, sauces, or utensils?
3. What name should I put on the order?
4. What is the best phone number?
5. What time would you like to pick it up?

If the caller has a question about allergens, a manager request, or something your menu does not cover, send it to staff. ROAL is built to do that. It takes catering inquiries, but it also knows when to hand a call off with a summary instead of guessing.

For related menu wording, see [combos and specials on the phone](/blog/combo-meals-phone-orders) and [telling callers about daily specials](/blog/daily-specials-phone). Those ideas can help if your catering menu includes party bundles or add-on specials.

sections.h2: How do I set up a catering menu so ROAL can read it correctly?
sections.body:
The easiest setup is the one that already makes sense to a caller. ROAL reads your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, then builds a phone host in about a minute from public menu pages, menu PDFs, or menu photos. You can also upload a menu in any format.

Before you go live, check these items:
- Every catering package has a clear name
- Serving counts are visible
- Prices are easy to find
- Add-ons are labeled simply
- Sold-out items are marked
- Hours and pickup notes are current

After setup, you can test-call the host in the browser with no sign-up needed. Then claim the host, get a phone line for each location, and forward your existing number when you want calls routed there. Forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered, depending on your setup.

If you need carrier forwarding instructions, confirm the exact code with your carrier and test it with a real call. Codes vary by plan and carrier. For many landlines and some carriers, *72 and *73 are common. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# and ##21# are used for all calls, while **61*number# and **67*number# may be used for unanswered or busy forwarding. Always verify first.

sections.h2: What’s the fastest way to clean up a catering menu this week?
sections.body:
You do not need a full redesign to make a restaurant catering menu easier to use. Start with the items that bring the most questions and clean up those first.

Use this 30-minute edit list:
1. Pick your top 5 catering items.
2. Rewrite each one with serving count, contents, and price first.
3. Remove extra words that do not help on the phone.
4. Add one note for utensils, lead time, or swaps.
5. Mark any sold-out items clearly.

A good test is simple: can a caller understand the item after hearing it once? If not, shorten it. If your staff has to explain the same tray three different ways, the menu needs cleanup.

This is also a good time to update your hours, FAQs, and any catering-specific notes in your dashboard. ROAL has a menu editor, call history with transcripts and recordings, and a place for questions the host could not answer. That makes it easier to tighten your catering wording over time.

If you want a quick starting point, [build a free test host](/try) from your website and listen to how your catering menu sounds on the phone. The goal is not fancy wording. The goal is a menu people can order from without guessing.

takeaways: Lead with serving count, contents, and price on every catering item.
Use short menu names that sound natural when spoken on the phone.
Keep add-ons, utensils, and lead times easy to find.
Send tricky catering questions to staff with a clear summary.
A phone-friendly menu helps callers place orders faster and with fewer corrections.

faq.q: What should be included in a restaurant catering menu?
faq.a: A restaurant catering menu should show the name of the item, how many people it feeds, what comes with it, the price, and any add-ons or extra charges. If callers often ask about utensils, bread, sauces, or lead time, include those too. The goal is to answer the most common questions before the caller has to ask.

faq.q: How detailed should catering menu descriptions be?
faq.a: Detailed enough to prevent confusion, but short enough to read on the phone. Most independent restaurants do better with one-line or two-line descriptions that include serving size, main items, and price. Long paragraphs are harder to understand when someone is ordering quickly.

faq.q: How do I make catering menu prices easier to understand?
faq.a: Keep the pricing pattern consistent. Put the base tray price first, then list add-ons in a simple way, like extra protein, extra sauce, or utensil packs. If a caller needs a total, give it back clearly before confirming the order.

ROAL can take catering inquiries and hand tricky ones to staff with a summary. It can collect items, sizes, modifiers, notes, caller name, phone number, and ready time, then confirm the order back. It does not take card numbers over the phone.
